full_text:
If I permit myself one bearish EthCC review tweet, it’s that the EF and ethCC leadership are very misguided on Ethereum (the Computer)’s decentralisation. Behind closed doors they are again trying to rush through issuance caps, and think Eth’s Nakamoto coefficient is the wrong measure of decentralisation. They care more about “hard money” and their tax bills than Ethereum being incorruptible. 

I think they misunderstand why Ethereum is valuable, as well as the purpose of stake and issuance:

You can make a blockchain with tiny issuance, but unless it’s decentralised no one will value it. You can change economic policy to favour the 0.4% of solo stakers, but they don’t control fork choice. You can claim $X billion dollars are enough economic security to prevent the manipulation of finality, but censoring what you attest to isn’t slashable so that doesn’t matter in practice despite mattering in theory.

Where I mostly agree with them is that any change of economics needs massive legitimacy, and I think lean Ethereum is a legitimate reason to rethink economics to ensure block building+proving is meaningfully decentralised. I think we agree that social slashing is not a realistic enough threat right now. I think we also (mostly) agree that a Nakamoto of 5 is far too low for the world computer (even if some dispute it being the most important measure). I think we also collectively believe that everyone with opinions on issuance are being genuine and mean the best for Ethereum, but are likely ‘feeling different parts of the elephant’. 

Constructive next steps are publishing credible data on the cost to operate stake, Ethereum’s Nakamoto coefficient, the gini index of its withdrawal credentials, R&D on EIPs that mitigate centralisation pressures, analysis of Ethereum’s principal agent problem in staking, and how we might 10x+ Ethereum’s decentralisation in a post-quantum future. 

A centralised Ethereum is the ultimate financial panopticon, is worse than the status quo, and is something I worry deeply about bringing into the world. I think the majority of Eth people agree and want to prevent that future. If so, we need to bring CROPS to the consensus layer, and not allow absolute power to corrupt absolutely; by no means an easy feat, but one I think we have rough consensus on vying for. Obol will remain steadfast on the front lines of this battle.

full_text: @OisinKyne I'm not EF/EthCC leadership, but I'd say it's misguided to believe you can prevent capture while allowing the staking ratio to rise to 100%. Ensuring sustainable issuance is the only way to achieve that. Excess issuance will not fix the Nakamoto coefficient, it makes things worse
name: pintail

full_text:
I agree that capture would be likely at 100%, I disagree that we get anywhere close in practice even if we change nothing. At the same time, I think we’ve a better chance of decent Nakamoto at a higher than comfortable ratio than at an artificially capped ratio. The cure is worse than the disease imo. 

A generous issuance curve was a deliberate choice to prevent the big orgs squeezing out the small ones. 95% of node operators don’t even feel the dilution effects because they’re not staking their own eth. (The principal agent problem I’m alluding to)

Issuance isn’t our only lever, we could make native staking suck less by introducing a price to exit stake (on an exponential curve/basefee), and adding EIP7716 correlated downtime penalties. Going further we could ship sublinear staking APRs if we thought our anti sybil mechanisms were good enough. Caps are our least effective fix imo if the success measure is Nakamoto not staking ratio. :)

full_text:
> There is no reason for growth to stop 

Of course there is, there’s an extremely long exit queue, inactivity penalties, operational costs, and the chance to lose some or all of your eth in a mass slashing. 

> no reason that small orgs would be favoured 
Not small orgs specifically, but the choice to print more eth rather than a fixed amount was to prevent the big stakers driving returns to minuscule in order to drive out smaller deployments by making them non economical. Now people deliberately want to set the curve to drive people out, but I contend that will most hurt the (economically rational*) long tail. (*A couple ideologues at the extreme will remain no matter what)

Source is verbal from @StakeETH who was involved in reviewing the curve and built the first economic model from the draft specs, not sure if there’s much written record of the rationale.

full_text:
> from the perspective of the principal 

Is that not the same for delegating to a CEX then? You don’t see the marginal effort involved in either? 

> bad faith 

I’m showing my bias/perspective sure but calling it bad faith is excessive imo. The plan is to drive the apr so low that those with higher cost bases opt to drop out. There’s not a guarantee that the smaller and more decentralised setups have a higher cost basis but it’s correlated enough that I don’t think my shorthand is bad faith. The big CEXs+ETFs aren’t the ones that will be leaving due to a cap. They have 100x lower per key operating costs than your 32 eth solo staker. 

> to be used without delegation 

The purpose of a system is what it does. Do you think >5% of stake self stakes? (ID’d solo stakers sit at 0.4%). Pretending the network isn’t what it is in practice is why we come to the wrong conclusions about dilution. I work harder than near anyone to get people to run their own nodes and squad stake, but we need to be clear eyed about the system if we want to improve it. Fixing native staking and implementing EIP 7716 (correlated downtime penalties) might incrementally improve self staking. Issuance caps won’t gain you any new solos (maybe it’ll slow the bleed of solos hurt by taxes, but thats fractions of a percent of the network, and I’m more worried about the Nakamoto side than how long the long tail is).

full_text:
I don’t think I’m misrepresenting things (lmk what you take issue with) nor is it obvious (at least to me) that my OP or subsequent tweets are in bad faith, I explicitly say I think everyone is genuine and advocating in Ethereum’s best interest. 

> None of what you’re proposing will improve long run Nakamoto 

I think correlation penalties for liveness penalties encourages minimising correlation (thus improving Nakamoto, but weakly admittedly)

I think a price to exit makes native staking more viable to stakers sensitive to the optionality of exiting. Making CEX and LST staking (marginally) less advantageous. 

I think correlation penalties might enable sub linear staking rewards for larger stake amounts, (but that’s the most exotic idea and not something near term). 

I think ‘excess issuance’ allows for more operators in the validator set, and makes discouragement attacks harder. More operators is a prerequisite for better Nakamoto (but no guarantee). FWIW A more important % than staking ratio is the median delegation fee but we don’t even go near that number in all this issuance discourse unfortunately. 

I agree that our social slashing deterrence is far too weak, but staking ratio isn’t the only determinant of if we could use it in practice. E.g. if we have a robust diverse staking set, slashing one bad actor is easier than if we have a duopoly validator set (in Nakamoto terms), social slashing is also a tall order then imo.

Do you think an issuance cap will improve Nakamoto (if so, how?), or just that a lower ratio is worth a potential deterioration of Nakamoto. (Presuming you don’t think caps will have 0 impact vs status quo Nakamoto)
